5	Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.

12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	**Three open**, all in the registry browser and all found while reviewing the
15	design for §3.8 rather than by a test; see [§1.3](#13-open). D1–D11 are fixed;
16	§1.1 records what each was and why the chosen fix was the right one.
17	
18	The five that stayed open longest — D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 — were parked not
19	because they were hard but because each altered something the user already saw,
20	so they needed a deliberate call rather than a drive-by fix. All five were then
21	decided together and fixed in one pass; see [§1.2](#12-the-five-parked-defects).
22	
23	### 1.1 Fixed
24	
25	**The command line took focus from the render path.** Found in phase 5.
26	`renderHeader` called `a.commandInput.Focus()` whenever `commandMode` was set —
27	a mutation inside `View()`, which Rule 110 makes read-only. A
28	`bubbles/textinput` drops every key it receives while blurred, so the command
29	line only accepted typing because a render happened to have run first. Focus is
30	now taken in `enterCommandMode` and released alongside the existing `Blur()`
31	calls on the way out. In production the ordering held, so nothing was visibly
32	broken; the coupling surfaced the moment a test drove the router without
33	rendering, and the same latent bug would bite anyone reordering the loop.
34	
35	**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
36	phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.
37	
38	The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
39	the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
40	was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
41	The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
42	without documenting it at all.
43	
44	The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
45	where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
46	stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.
47	
48	`explorer` made it four in a row, though only just: every key was documented
49	except `/`. The check caught it on its first run.
50	
51	`security` broke the streak — its help documents every key its header
52	advertises, across all four states.
53	
54	`oci_resources` then produced the worst instance, in phase 4. The Networks and
55	Volumes tabs documented `n` for a binding that has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111
56	renamed it — the same drift `status` and `workspaces` carried — but the **whole
57	Registries tab was undocumented**: `ctrl+n`, `e`, `l` and `L` appeared nowhere,
58	so four actions on a tab were reachable only by guessing.
59	
60	That view needed one adjustment to the check: its help qualifies most keys with
61	the tab they belong to (`enter (Images)`, `ctrl+n (Networks)`), so the
62	parenthetical comes off before matching. That convention is worth keeping — with
63	four tabs sharing a keymap, an unqualified `enter` would be ambiguous.
64	
65	So the pattern across five views: the drift is a Rule 111 rename the help did
66	not follow, plus whole surfaces added later and never documented at all.
67	
68	All five are fixed, and every view in `internal/ui` now asserts that each key
69	`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
70	have caught the drift when it was introduced.
71	
72	**The explorer acted on a different row than the one highlighted.** Found in
73	phase 3, and the most serious defect the coverage work has turned up.
74	
75	`handleKeyMsg` resolved the cursor against `sortedItems(currentItems())` — the
76	unfiltered list — while the table was built from the filtered one. With a filter
77	active the two indices disagree, so `ctrl+d`, `p`, `→` and `ctrl+w` all acted on
78	whatever happened to sit at that index in the *unfiltered* list. Filtering to a
79	single project and pressing `ctrl+d` scheduled a different group for deletion.
80	`GetShortcuts` had it too, so even the advertised `ctrl+w` keyed off the wrong
81	node.
82	
83	Both now go through `visibleItems()`, the single list `updateTableRows` builds
84	from. Pinned by `TestActionsResolveTheRowTheUserCanSee`, which filters to a row
85	that sits at a different index in each list — the fixtures were chosen so the
86	two cannot coincide.
87	
88	**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
89	clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
90	fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
91	highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
92	until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.
93	
94	The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
95	change; workspaces had no equivalent. **`explorer` had it too**, and only on the
96	filter path — its drill-down was already safe because it calls `GotoTop()`.
97	Fixed the same way.
98	
99	**Two tabs reported nothing when Docker was down.** Found in phase 4.
100	`handleImagesList` has always set a footer message on failure;
101	`handleNetworksList` and `handleVolumesList` only logged, so with the daemon
102	stopped those two tabs showed an empty table — indistinguishable from "you have
103	no networks". Both now match their sibling.
104	
105	**The Registries tab opened empty.** `switchTab` focused the table and fired the
106	`docker login` status check, but never called `updateRegistryTable()` — so the
107	tab stayed blank until an asynchronous Docker call answered, even though the
108	registries come from the config file and were available immediately.
109	
110	**A search counter with no floor.** `RegistryBrowser.AddRegistryTags`
111	decremented `pendingSearches` unconditionally. A duplicate or late response drove
112	it negative, and the *next* search then started from that base: `IsSearching()`
113	stayed false while requests were genuinely in flight, so the spinner never
114	showed. Floored at zero.
115	
116	**Footer messages with no timer.** `explorer.handleDeleteComplete` set
117	`footerError` and returned `nil`, so a failed delete left "Delete failed — check
118	logs" on screen until something else overwrote it. Rule 128 caps footer messages
119	at three seconds, and the same file's `BrowserOpenedMsg` handler already did it
120	correctly. Now returns `clearFooterErrorCmd()`.
121	
122	The security view had it worse: **Rule 128 was not honoured anywhere in it.**
123	`statusMessage` was set in three places — "Added x to .gitleaksignore", "Failed
124	to ignore secret", "No references available" — and there was no clear timer in
125	the package at all, so whichever happened last stayed on screen until a tab
126	switch happened to reset it. `clearStatusCmd` / `clearStatusMsg` added and all
127	three wired, pinned by `TestFooterMessagesExpire`.
128	
129	**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
130	"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
131	unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
132	independent defects with no shared code.
133	
134	`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
135	normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
136	Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
137	`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
138	silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
139	(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
140	first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
141	that treats it as one.
142	
143	The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
144	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
145	navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
146	line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
147	confusing than one that is plainly not there.
148	
149	The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
150	cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
151	was guarding.
152	
153	Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
154	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
155	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
156	confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
157	`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
158	alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.
159	
160	**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
161	looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
162	fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.
163	
164	Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
165	`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
166	the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
167	terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
168	ones.
169	
170	A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
171	in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
172	Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
173	gone.
174	
175	A **sixth site** closed the family out, in the last package of phase 3:
176	`parseVersion` in `internal/ui/security` truncated its fallback with
177	`result[:15]`. Version strings are ASCII in practice, so this was the
178	lowest-risk of the six — but it is the same pattern, and it is now
179	`theme.TruncateWidth`. Grepping for `[:` on strings across `internal/ui` now
180	returns nothing but slice indexing.
181	
182	The same function had a second defect: it scanned for the version number by
183	taking the first whitespace-separated token starting with `v`, so
184	`gitleaks version 8.18.2` reported its version as **"version"**. A leading `v`
185	now only counts when a digit follows it.
186	
187	A **fifth site** turned up during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
188	`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
189	results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
190	could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
191	`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
192	Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.
193	
194	The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
195	(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
196	`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).
197	
198	One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
199	`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
200	so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
201	theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.
202	
203	**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
204	planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.
205	
206	The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
207	credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
208	unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
209	credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
210	same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
211	won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
212	after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
213	strips the path before the helper is ever called.
214	
215	**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
216	the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
217	change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
218	`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.
219	
220	Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
221	path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
222	contexts anyway.
223	
224	Two smaller defects went with it:
225	
226	- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
227	  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
228	  hang indefinitely.
229	- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
230	  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
231	  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
232	  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.
233	
234	`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
235	than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
236	`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
237	common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
238	`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
239	`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.
240	
241	### 1.2 The five parked defects
242	
243	D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 were each recorded rather than fixed on discovery,
244	because each changed something the user already saw. They were decided together
245	and fixed in one pass. Three of the five had a test written to fail *on the
246	fix*, and all three did.
247	
248	**D4 — `tab` navigated the delete confirmation.** Rule 135 reserves `tab` for
249	switching tabs and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively; the modal
250	had it exactly inverted, cycling on `tab` and clamping on `↑ / ↓`. `↑ / ↓` now
251	cycle, which is what keeps every control reachable in one direction, and the
252	`tab` cases are gone. The explorer no longer advertises "tab Navigate" while the
253	modal is open, and `↑↓` is not advertised in its place — Rule 138 calls it
254	obvious. The permanent variant still skips its locked checkbox, so cycling there
255	toggles between the two buttons.
256	
257	**D8 — write-only CRUD flags.** `creating`, `editing` and `confirming` were
258	assigned in five places and read in none, and `ComponentFormCancelledMsg` — the
259	only thing that would have reset two of them — could never be sent. Deleted, all
260	of it. Nothing else changed: the phase 2 tests had deliberately asserted on
261	`componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags, which is what made
262	this safe a phase later.
263	
264	**D9 — the containers list opened Z→A.** `New()` set neither `sortColumn` nor
265	`sortAsc`, so both took their zero value. Both are now set explicitly, so the
266	default is stated rather than inherited. `TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending`
267	became `TestDefaultSortIsNameAscending`, and the cycle test walks forward from
268	ascending. The `loadedModel` helper still sets the sort itself even though it
269	now matches the constructor: those tests should say which order they rely on.
270	
271	**D10 — a registry failure was invisible.** `renderTemplateList` returned early
272	when the field was unfocused and the warning sat below that return, so a form
273	opened after the OCI registry failed offered a Template field reading "none"
274	with nothing to distinguish "the registry is down" from "there are no
275	templates". The warning moved into `renderTemplateWarning` and is appended in
276	both branches — it explains why the list is empty, so it belongs wherever the
277	list is.
278	
279	**D11 — CRITICAL and HIGH rendered identically.** `getSeverityStyle` composed
280	CRITICAL by hand as `ColorError` + `Bold`, which is byte-for-byte the
281	`theme.StatusErrorStyle` it returned for HIGH. The palette moved to
282	`theme.SeverityTextStyle`, next to the `TableStylesForSeverity` it draws from,
283	and the view delegates (Rule 102). An unrecognised severity now falls back to
284	the info colour rather than to `DimStyle`, so it is still legible.
285	
286	The pattern worth keeping: when a defect is recorded rather than fixed, write
287	the test **inverted** — asserting the current behaviour and saying so. D9, D10
288	and D11 each had one, and each failed the moment the fix landed, which is how
289	the stale test and the stale backlog entry got found together.
290	
291	### 1.3 Open
292	
293	D12–D14 sit in `internal/ui/oci_resources` and are cheap on their own, but
294	§3.8 rewrites the code path each of them lives in. Fix them **as part of** that
295	work rather than ahead of it, and write each one's test inverted first, per the
296	pattern above.
297	
298	D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 router pass and are unrelated to §3.8. Each
299	has an inverted test asserting the current behaviour, named in its entry.
300	
301	**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery.** The flag is
302	honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
303	`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
304	path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
305	(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
306	unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
307	`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
308	`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
309	still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
310	on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
311	host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
312	`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
313	say "do not send credentials here" at all.
314	
315	**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
316	`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
317	(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
318	unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
319	concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
320	seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
321	on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
322	the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
323	resolve and the form renders immediately.
324	
325	A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
326	`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
327	registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
328	the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.
329	
330	**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
331	`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
332	searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
333	Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
334	returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
335	in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
336	preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
337	gains a group level at the same time.
338	
339	**D15 — `esc` never reaches a view that is not editing.** `handleKeyMsg`
340	(`keys.go`) answers `esc` itself through `maybeQuitCommandMode`, which forwards
341	the key only when the view reports `InEditMode()`. Every other time the router
342	consumes it and returns a resize. The explorer's `esc` → `handleDrillUp`
343	(`update.go:157`) is therefore dead code: only `←` and `h` drill up, though
344	Rule 111 lists `esc` as the third way. The explorer's own unit tests pass
345	because they drive the model directly, bypassing the router — this is precisely
346	the class of defect router tests exist to catch.
347	
348	The security view already works around it: `InEditMode()` there is documented as
349	*"returns true when the view needs to handle ESC key"*, which overloads a
350	predicate about focused fields into a predicate about key ownership. The fix is
351	to give `esc` the same shape as every other key — forward it to the view first
352	and let the router act only if the view did not — but that changes behaviour in
353	every view at once, so it wants its own commit and a pass over each view's esc
354	handling. Inverted test:
355	`TestEscIsSwallowedForAViewThatIsNotEditing` (`router_test.go`).
356	
357	**D16 — `:netdiag` is documented but not accepted.** `CLAUDE.md` lists
358	"`netdiag` or `net`", the view is named `netdiag` throughout, and the directory
359	is `internal/ui/netdiag` — but `viewMap` in `parser.go` has only `"net"`.
360	`:netdiag` parses to `CommandUnknown`, which leaves the command line open with
361	no diagnostic. One map entry. Covered by the comment on the `net` row in
362	`TestEveryNamedViewCanBeReached` (`command_line_test.go`).
363	
364	**D17 — the completion catalogue is a subset of the parser.**
365	`buildCommands()` (`completion.go`) lists eight full commands; the parser
366	accepts fourteen views plus aliases. `gitlab-explorer`, `workspaces`,
367	`security` and `net` all work when typed in full but cannot be tab-completed,
368	and nothing keeps the two lists in step. The parser's `viewMap` is the natural
369	single source — the catalogue should be derived from it rather than restated.
370	Worth doing with D16, which is the same drift.
371	
372	**D18 — the header overflows a narrow window.** `buildShortcutLines`
373	(`app_header.go:202`) intends to clip the shortcut block to its column —
374	`// Truncate if wider than col2Width` — but calls `theme.PadWithBg`, which
375	returns the content untouched when it is already at or past the target. Below
376	roughly 100 columns the header therefore renders wider than the window and
377	wraps: at width 80 with twelve shortcuts every header row comes out 95 wide.
378	The fix is `lipgloss.NewStyle().MaxWidth(col2Width)`, which truncates without
379	cutting an escape sequence in half — the hazard Rule 122 is about. Inverted
380	test: `TestANarrowHeaderOverflowsTheWindow` (`header_test.go`).
381	
382	**D19 — the Trivy command shown is not the one run.** `GetTrivyCommand` exists
383	to display what will be executed, and rebuilds the argument list by hand from
384	the same inputs as `RunTrivy`. The two have drifted: `RunTrivy` takes
385	`ignoreEOL` and appends `--ignore-status end_of_life`; `GetTrivyCommand` does
386	not take the parameter at all. A user copying the logged command gets different
387	results from the scan they just watched. `RunTrivyMisconfig` and `GenerateSBOM`
388	have no display counterpart at all, so their commands are never shown.
389	
390	The fix is not to add the missing flag but to remove the duplication: extract
391	one pure `trivyArgs(...)` builder returning the binary name and its arguments,
392	and have `RunTrivy` turn it into an `exec.Cmd` while `GetTrivyCommand` joins it
393	into a string. Same for gitleaks. This is planned as the split step of phase 5
394	for `internal/scan`, since it is also what makes the argument surface testable.

993	#### Why `alt+`, not `ctrl+`
994	
995	`ctrl+:` cannot be made to work, and this is the note that should stop anyone
996	reintroducing it. A terminal encodes Ctrl by clearing bits, which only covers
997	ASCII `@` through `_` (0x40–0x5F). `:` is 0x3A: Ctrl+: sends a plain `:` or
998	nothing. Reporting it as a distinct key needs the Kitty keyboard protocol or
999	xterm's `modifyOtherKeys`, and bubbletea v1.3.10 implements neither. A
1000	`case "ctrl+:"` would be dead code.
1001	
1002	Alt has no such limit — a terminal sends ESC then the key, and bubbletea reports
1003	that as the key carrying `Alt`. The alternative considered was a free
1004	`ctrl+<letter>` (`b g l p t u v x z` are unused; `ctrl+i m j h [` are Tab, Enter,
1005	LF, Backspace and Esc and must be left alone), which is marginally more portable
1006	but loses the `:` in the gesture.

1209	### 3.9 Every secret goes to a host secret manager, and radio buttons go away
1210

1212	three of the five storage paths are exactly that, and the option the UI labels
1213	"secure" is one of them.

1216	one storage path, the choice the radios present stops existing.

1218	#### Where secrets go today
1219	
1220	| Secret | Destination | Protection |
1221	|---|---|---|
1222	| Forge token | `~/.devdesk/credentials-<ctx>.json` | **plaintext JSON**, 0600 |
1223	| Forge token | `gitlab.token` in `contexts/<ctx>/config.yaml` | **plaintext YAML** |
1224	| Forge token | git credential helper | whatever the helper does |
1225	| Registry password | `~/.docker/config.json` via `docker login` | whatever Docker's `credsStore` does |

1228	`RegistryItem` is the one part that already gets this right: it has no password
1229	field by construction, and the multi-registry code relies on `docker login`
1230	instead. The legacy `RegistryConfig.Password` is the outlier, and it is still
1231	read.

1233	#### The option labelled "secure" is not
1234	
1235	`ChainStorage.Save` writes to **every** storage in the chain
1236	(`credentials/storage.go:37`), and all three construction sites build it as
1237	`NewChainStorage(FileStorage, GitCredentialStorage)` (`app.go:245`, `:383`,
1238	`:1483`). So choosing **"Save to Git Credential Manager (secure)"** stores the
1239	token in the credential manager *and* in
1240	`~/.devdesk/credentials-<context>.json` in plaintext. The label is not merely
1241	optimistic, it is wrong about the option it describes.
1242	
1243	Reads make it worse. `FileStorage` is **first** in the chain and
1244	`ChainStorage.Load` returns the first hit, so the plaintext file is
1245	authoritative and the credential manager is never consulted while that file
1246	exists. The secure backend is decorative in both directions.
1247	
1248	The other option is no better, in a different way: **"Save token to config file
1249	(less secure)"** sets `saveToHelper = false` (`auth/update.go:213`), so nothing
1250	reaches the chain at all and the token lands only in `config.yaml`. Both
1251	options put the token in plaintext on disk; the "secure" one does it twice.

1253	**And logout does not clean up.** `handleLogoutComplete` (`auth/update.go:191`)
1254	clears `m.config.GitLab.Token` in memory with no `config.Save` behind it, so the
1255	token survives in `contexts/<ctx>/config.yaml`. `ChainStorage.Delete` does clear
1256	both storages, so the credentials file copy goes — the config copy does not.

1258	#### What "host secret manager" can honestly promise
1259	
1260	The distinction that decides the design: delegating to `git credential`
1261	delegates to **whatever helper git happens to be configured with**. If that is
1262	`store`, the token lands in `~/.git-credentials` in plaintext — the same
1263	failure, relocated. `cache` keeps it in memory only. Only `manager` (GCM),
1264	`osxkeychain` and `libsecret` reach a real OS store. So "goes through git
1265	credential" is not the same claim as "encrypted at rest", and the requirement
1266	above is the second one.
1267	
1268	| Route | Gets | Costs |
1269	|---|---|---|
1270	| **A — keep `git credential`, inspect the helper** | no new dependency; reuses machinery just hardened for context isolation (§1.1) | must read `git config credential.helper` and refuse or warn on `store` and on empty; still trusts the user's git config |
1271	| **B — talk to the OS store directly** (`zalando/go-keyring`: wincred / Keychain / Secret Service, no cgo; or `99designs/keyring` for more backends) | guarantees the store; independent of git configuration | a dependency, and new failure modes — no D-Bus in a headless Linux session being the usual one |

1273	**Recommendation: B as the primary path, A kept as an explicit alternative** for
1274	users who want their tokens where GCM already puts everything else. Only B can
1275	promise what the requirement asks; A is the pragmatic option and should stay
1276	reachable, not become the default.

1319	set**, and that checkboxes remain for independent booleans.
1320	
1321	#### Sketch of the work
1322	
1323	1. Add `KeyringStorage` over the OS store, and a probe that reports whether one
1324	   is reachable. Route A becomes a second implementation of the same interface.
1325	2. Delete `FileStorage` and `NewFileStorageForContext`. This is the change that
1326	   makes the "secure" label true, and nothing else in the chain matters until it
1327	   is gone.
1328	3. Replace `ChainStorage` with explicit selection — store, else git credential
1329	   if configured with a real helper, else memory with a warning. Writing to
1330	   every backend at once is what produced the current defect; keep one
1331	   destination.
1332	4. Remove `GitLabConfig.Token` and `RegistryConfig.Password`, with the migration
1333	   sweep on load.
1334	5. Persist the logout: clear the store *and* save the config.

1336	
1337	Steps 2 and 5 are small and fix live defects; they need none of the rest.
1338	
1339	---
1340	
1341	### 3.10 An inference-backed explainer for network diagnostics
1342	
1343	Netdiag runs the tests but leaves the interpretation to the user. The first —
1344	and for now only — AI feature is an **explainer over diagnostic results that
1345	DevDesk already holds**. It sends a few kilobytes of structured facts, needs no
1346	new privilege, and touches no packet payload.
1347	
1348	#### Settled
1349	
1350	| # | Question | Decision |
1351	|---|---|---|
1352	| 1 | Scope of v1 | **Explainer only.** No capture. tcpdump is a later input to the same explainer, not part of this. |
1353	| 2 | Local server lifecycle | **DevDesk consumes an endpoint.** It never starts, stops or supervises an inference server. |
1354	| 3 | Protocol | **One OpenAI-compatible client** (`POST /v1/chat/completions`). Covers ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio and hosted providers. No second native client. |
1355	| 4 | Redaction | **Nothing sensitive reaches a model, local or remote.** Not a per-provider policy — one rule, no exception for `localhost`. |
1356	| 5 | Snaplen | Headers-only is the default **when capture arrives**. Out of scope for v1 by decision 1. |
1357	| 6 | Provider scope | **One per context.** |
1358	
1359	Decisions 2 and 6 cost nothing. Consuming an endpoint means the provider is a
1360	URL, a model name and a token — a `AIConfig` block in the context's
1361	`config.yaml`, which is per-context by construction. The token goes to the store
1362	from §3.9 like any other; it must never land in the YAML. The GPU question that
1363	motivated hosting (Docker on macOS runs a Linux VM with no Metal access, so
1364	unified memory is unreachable from a container) disappears with it: the user
1365	runs `ollama serve` natively, or a container, or nothing, and DevDesk does not
1366	care.
1367	
1368	#### The hard part is decision 4, and Presidio only half-answers it
1369	
1370	Reference: [Docker agent PII protection with
1371	Presidio](https://k33g.org/p/20260716-docker-agent-pii-protection-presidio) —
1372	an analyzer/anonymizer pair behind HTTP, hooked on `before_llm_call`, replacing
1373	detected spans with typed tokens.
1374	
1375	Two things transfer and one does not.
1376	
1377	**What does not transfer: the entity set.** Presidio detects *PII* — names,
1378	emails, phone numbers, credit cards, IBANs, national IDs, IP addresses. What
1379	DevDesk holds is mostly not PII: internal hostnames, private ranges, resolver
1380	addresses, listening sockets and process names, registry and forge URLs,
1381	Gitleaks matches. `IP_ADDRESS` is the only real overlap. A DevDesk payload could
1382	pass Presidio clean while still describing the whole internal network. Presidio
1383	is therefore a **second net, not the mechanism**.
1384	
1385	**What transfers: fail-closed, and the deterministic layers.** The post notes
1386	its own default is fail-open and that production needs `PII_FAIL_CLOSED=1`.
1387	Given §3.9, fail-closed is the only acceptable mode here: if the redactor is
1388	unreachable, nothing is sent, and the user is told why. And the post's two
1389	non-NER layers — a deny-list and structural rules by column — are the parts
1390	that actually caught things reliably. That is the direction to build in.
1391	
1392	#### Allow-list construction beats scrubbing
1393	
1394	The post scrubs because it hooks arbitrary agent traffic and cannot know what is
1395	in it. DevDesk is not in that position: it **assembles the payload itself** from
1396	`m.results`, which is already typed and structured. So the payload should be
1397	built field by field from an explicit allow-list, not produced as a blob and
1398	then cleaned.
1399	
1400	The difference matters: **a field never included cannot fail to be redacted.**
1401	Scrubbing is a filter that can miss; construction is a whitelist that cannot.
1402	Presidio then runs over the assembled payload as a check on the construction,
1403	and any hit is a bug in the allow-list, not a routine save.
1404	
1405	#### The tension: the sensitive data *is* the diagnostic data
1406	
1407	Redacting addresses out of a network diagnostic destroys the diagnostic. A model
1408	told `[IP_REDACTED]` resolves to `[IP_REDACTED]` can conclude nothing, and the
1409	answer that comes back is unreadable.
1410	
1411	The resolution is **consistent pseudonymisation that preserves the analytically
1412	relevant class**, not blanket redaction:
1413	
1414	| Real | Sent | Preserved |
1415	|---|---|---|
1416	| `api.corp.internal` | `host-1` | identity across the payload |
1417	| `10.2.3.4` | `private-a` | RFC1918, and same-subnet relations |
1418	| `203.0.113.9` | `public-b` | routable, distinct from private |
1419	| `10.2.3.7` | `private-c` | same /24 as `private-a` |
1420	
1421	The hypotheses the model is asked to rank depend on structure — private vs
1422	public, same subnet or not, resolves or not, port open or filtered, which TLS
1423	stage failed — never on the literal octets. So this loses nothing. "host-1
1424	resolves to private-a but hop 5 is public-c, so the route leaves your network"
1425	is exactly as useful as the version with real addresses.
1426	
1427	The mapping stays in memory, and the response is **restored locally before
1428	display**, so the user reads real names. The blog post does not do this
1429	round-trip — its tokens are one-way — but DevDesk needs it, because unlike a
1430	CSV of customers its payload is *entirely* made of identifiers.
1431	
1432	#### Confirmation before send
1433	
1434	The assembled, pseudonymised payload is rendered in the viewport before it
1435	leaves, for every provider. Decision 4 says local and remote are treated alike,
1436	so there is no "trusted endpoint" shortcut. This costs one keypress and is what
1437	makes the feature auditable without reading the source.
1438	
1439	#### Bubble Tea shape
1440	
1441	Streaming is the only delicate part. Rule 110 forbids mutating the model inside
1442	a `Cmd`, so the pattern is a channel plus a `Cmd` that reads one chunk and
1443	returns a `streamChunkMsg{gen, text}` which re-arms itself — the same shape as
1444	the spinner, reusing the generation counter already in `run.go:33` to discard a
1445	superseded stream.
1446	
1447	Cancellation is mandatory, not optional: a local model on CPU can take minutes.
1448	A `context.CancelFunc` lives in the model and `esc` cancels. **D13 is the
1449	warning** — a state the user cannot leave while something resolves is a defect
1450	this repository already has once.
1451	
1452	No new view and no command. The explanation is a results tab under the table
1453	(Rule 123), triggered by a key on the results screen. A dedicated view turns
1454	this into a chat product, which is not what is being asked for. With no provider
1455	configured the shortcut is absent rather than erroring (Rule 130), and all
1456	strings are English US (Rule 129).
1457	
1458	#### Sketch of the work
1459	
1460	1. `internal/ai`: config block, an OpenAI-compatible client behind a small
1461	   interface so tests inject a fake — the `runner` indirection in
1462	   `internal/docker` is the precedent — and the token read from the §3.9 store.
1463	2. The payload builder: allow-listed fields out of `m.results`, plus the
1464	   pseudonymiser and its inverse. Table-driven tests, like the existing
1465	   `dns_formatter` and `traceroute_formatter` parsers. **This is the feature; do
1466	   it first and it is testable with no endpoint at all.**
1467	3. The prompt: observed facts only, and an instruction to name which test each
1468	   claim rests on. The raw results stay on screen next to the explanation —
1469	   the narrative never replaces the data.
1470	4. Streaming, cancellation, and the results tab.
1471	5. The confirmation pane.
1472	6. Optional and last: Presidio as a fail-closed second net over the assembled
1473	   payload, behind a config flag. Two containers and a spaCy model is heavy
1474	   for a few kilobytes of already-structured text, and step 2 is what actually
1475	   provides the guarantee.
1476	
1477	Later, and explicitly not now: capture as an additional input (bounded by `-c`
1478	and `-G`, `-s 96` by default so payloads cannot be captured at all), and the
1479	deterministic flow summariser that would have to precede it — a pcap does not
1480	fit in a context window, and once the summariser exists it answers most of the
1481	question without a model. `nicolaka/netshoot` (`config.go:218`) already ships
1482	`tcpdump` and `tshark`, and the privileged host-namespace runner exists
1483	(`ports.go:36`, `topology.go:47`), so the missing piece is the analysis, not the
1484	plumbing.
1485	
1486	Adjacent candidates, ranked, none settled: Trivy remediation (§3.2 — low
1487	sensitivity, but any suggested base-image bump must be verified by a re-scan,

1489	highest risk since the payload *is* the secret — possibly viable by sending rule

116	// CountFindings aggregates findings into separate counters by source and severity.
117	// CVEs (source "trivy") are counted by severity into Counts.
118	// Secrets (source "gitleaks"), licenses ("trivy-license"), and misconfigs ("trivy-misconfig")
119	// are counted into their respective dedicated fields.
120	func (r *Result) CountFindings() {
121		r.Counts = SeverityCounts{}
122		r.SecretCount = 0
123		r.LicenseCount = 0
124		r.MisconfigCount = 0
125		for _, f := range r.Findings {
126			switch f.Source {
127			case "gitleaks":
128				r.SecretCount++
129			case "trivy-license":
130				r.LicenseCount++
131			case "trivy-misconfig":
132				r.MisconfigCount++
133			default: // "trivy" and any unknown source → CVE counts by severity
134				switch f.Severity {
135				case SeverityCritical:
136					r.Counts.Critical++
137				case SeverityHigh:
138					r.Counts.High++
139				case SeverityMedium:
140					r.Counts.Medium++
141				case SeverityLow:
142					r.Counts.Low++
143				default:
144					r.Counts.Unknown++
145				}
146			}
147		}
148	}

153			r.SecretCount + r.LicenseCount + r.MisconfigCount
154	}

184	// CheckDependenciesWithImages verifies tools with custom Docker images
185	func CheckDependenciesWithImages(trivyImage, gitleaksImage string) DependencyStatus {
186		// Use defaults if not specified
187		if trivyImage == "" {
188			trivyImage = DefaultTrivyImage
189		}
190		if gitleaksImage == "" {
191			gitleaksImage = DefaultGitleaksImage
192		}
193	
194		status := DependencyStatus{
195			TrivySource:    ToolSourceNone,
196			TrivyImage:     trivyImage,
197			GitleaksSource: ToolSourceNone,
198			GitleaksImage:  gitleaksImage,
199		}
200	
201		// Check if Docker is available
202		if path, err := exec.LookPath("docker"); err == nil && path != "" {
203			status.DockerAvailable = true
204		}
205	
206		// Check Trivy binary first
207		if path, err := exec.LookPath("trivy"); err == nil && path != "" {
208			status.TrivyAvailable = true
209			status.TrivySource = ToolSourceBinary
210			if out, err := exec.Command("trivy", "--version").Output(); err == nil {
211				status.TrivyVersion = string(out)
212			}
213		} else if status.DockerAvailable {
214			// Check for Trivy Docker image
215			if checkDockerImage(trivyImage) {
216				status.TrivyAvailable = true
217				status.TrivySource = ToolSourceDocker
218				// Get version from Docker image
219				if out, err := exec.Command("docker", "run", "--rm", trivyImage, "--version").Output(); err == nil {
220					status.TrivyVersion = "docker:" + string(out)
221				} else {
222					status.TrivyVersion = "docker"
223				}
224			}
225		}
226	
227		// Check Gitleaks binary first
228		if path, err := exec.LookPath("gitleaks"); err == nil && path != "" {
229			status.GitleaksAvailable = true
230			status.GitleaksSource = ToolSourceBinary
231			if out, err := exec.Command("gitleaks", "version").Output(); err == nil {
232				status.GitleaksVersion = string(out)
233			}
234		} else if status.DockerAvailable {
235			// Check for Gitleaks Docker image
236			if checkDockerImage(gitleaksImage) {
237				status.GitleaksAvailable = true
238				status.GitleaksSource = ToolSourceDocker
239				// Get version from Docker image
240				if out, err := exec.Command("docker", "run", "--rm", gitleaksImage, "version").Output(); err == nil {
241					status.GitleaksVersion = "docker:" + string(out)
242				} else {
243					status.GitleaksVersion = "docker"
244				}
245			}
246		}
247	
248		return status
249	}

253		cmd := exec.Command("docker", "images", "-q", image)
254		output, err := cmd.Output()
255		if err != nil {
256			return false
257		}

281	// Scan performs a security scan on the target, running all enabled stages in parallel.
282	func (s *Scanner) Scan(ctx context.Context, target string, targetType TargetType) (*Result, error) {
283		result := &Result{
284			Target:     target,
285			TargetType: targetType,
286			StartTime:  time.Now(),
287			Findings:   []Finding{},
288			Errors:     []string{},
289		}
290	
291		notify := func(update ProgressUpdate) {
292			if s.options.OnProgress != nil {
293				s.options.OnProgress(update)
294			}
295		}
296	
297		// mu guards writes to result (Findings, Errors, SBOMPath) from concurrent goroutines
298		var mu sync.Mutex
299	
300		eg, egCtx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
301	
302		// Vuln scan (Trivy)
303		if s.options.EnableVuln && s.deps.TrivyAvailable {
304			eg.Go(func() error {
305				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageRunning})
306				progressFn := func(detail string) {
307					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
308				}
309				cmd := GetTrivyCommand(target, targetType, false, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.IgnoreEOL)
310				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
311				findings, err := RunTrivy(egCtx, target, targetType, false, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
312				mu.Lock()
313				defer mu.Unlock()
314				if err != nil {
315					result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("trivy vuln: %v", err))
316					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageError, Detail: err.Error()})
317				} else {
318					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
319					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageDone})
320				}
321				return nil
322			})
323		}
324	
325		// License scan (Trivy, directory only)
326		if s.options.EnableLicense && s.deps.TrivyAvailable && targetType == TargetDirectory {
327			eg.Go(func() error {
328				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageRunning})
329				progressFn := func(detail string) {
330					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
331				}
332				cmd := GetTrivyCommand(target, targetType, true, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.IgnoreEOL)
333				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
334				findings, err := RunTrivy(egCtx, target, targetType, true, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
335				mu.Lock()
336				defer mu.Unlock()
337				if err != nil {
338					result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("trivy license: %v", err))
339					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageError})
340				} else {
341					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
342					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageDone})
343				}
344				return nil
345			})
346		}
347	
348		// Misconfig scan (Trivy)
349		if s.options.EnableMisconfig && s.deps.TrivyAvailable {
350			eg.Go(func() error {
351				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageRunning})
352				progressFn := func(detail string) {
353					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
354				}
355				findings, err := RunTrivyMisconfig(egCtx, target, targetType, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
356				mu.Lock()
357				defer mu.Unlock()
358				if err != nil {
359					result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("trivy misconfig: %v", err))
360					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageError})
361				} else {
362					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
363					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageDone})
364				}
365				return nil
366			})
367		}
368	
369		// Secret scan (Gitleaks, directory only)
370		if s.options.EnableSecret && s.deps.GitleaksAvailable && targetType == TargetDirectory {
371			eg.Go(func() error {
372				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets", Status: StageRunning})
373				progressFn := func(detail string) {
374					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
375				}
376				cmd := GetGitleaksCommand(target, s.deps.GitleaksSource, s.deps.GitleaksImage, s.options.GitleaksHistory, s.options.GitleaksConfig)
377				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
378				findings, err := RunGitleaks(egCtx, target, s.deps.GitleaksSource, s.deps.GitleaksImage, s.options.GitleaksHistory, s.options.GitleaksConfig, progressFn)
379				mu.Lock()
380				defer mu.Unlock()
381				if err != nil {
382					result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("gitleaks: %v", err))
383					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets", Status: StageError})
384				} else {
385					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
386					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets", Status: StageDone})
387				}
388				return nil
389			})
390		}
391	
392		// SBOM generation (Trivy)
393		if s.options.GenerateSBOM && s.deps.TrivyAvailable {
394			eg.Go(func() error {
395				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "sbom", Label: "SBOM", Status: StageRunning})
396				sbomPath, err := GenerateSBOM(egCtx, target, targetType, s.deps.TrivySource, s.deps.TrivyImage, s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.SBOMOutputDir)
397				mu.Lock()
398				defer mu.Unlock()
399				if err != nil {
400					result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("sbom: %v", err))
401					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "sbom", Label: "SBOM", Status: StageError})
402				} else {
403					result.SBOMPath = sbomPath
404					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "sbom", Label: "SBOM", Status: StageDone})
405				}
406				return nil
407			})
408		}
409	
410		// All goroutines return nil, so eg.Wait() never returns an error
411		_ = eg.Wait()
412	
413		result.EndTime = time.Now()
414		result.Duration = result.EndTime.Sub(result.StartTime)
415		result.CountFindings()
416	
417		return result, nil
418	}

90	// runTrivy executes a built invocation and parses what it wrote to stdout.
91	//
92	// A non-zero exit is not on its own a failure: Trivy exits 1 when it finds
93	// vulnerabilities, and the report on stdout is exactly what the caller asked
94	// for. Only an exit that produced no report is reported as an error.
95	func runTrivy(ctx context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]Finding, error) {
96		stdout, err := runner.Run(ctx, tc, progressFn)
97		if err != nil {
98			var exit *exitError
99			if !errors.As(err, &exit) || len(stdout) == 0 {
100				return nil, fmt.Errorf("trivy failed: %w", err)
101			}
102		}
103		return parseTrivyOutput(stdout)

106	// parseTrivyOutput parses Trivy JSON output into findings
107	func parseTrivyOutput(data []byte) ([]Finding, error) {
108		var report TrivyReport
109		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &report); err != nil {
110			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse trivy output: %w", err)
111		}
112	
113		var findings []Finding
114	
115		for _, result := range report.Results {
116			// Process vulnerabilities
117			for _, vuln := range result.Vulnerabilities {
118				// Build references from PrimaryURL and advisory links
119				refs := make([]string, 0, len(vuln.References)+1)
120				if vuln.PrimaryURL != "" {
121					refs = append(refs, vuln.PrimaryURL)
122				}
123				for _, r := range vuln.References {
124					if r != vuln.PrimaryURL {
125						refs = append(refs, r)
126					}
127				}
128	
129				// Build a fix command suggestion when a fixed version is known
130				fixCmd := ""
131				if vuln.FixedVersion != "" {
132					fixCmd = fmt.Sprintf("Update %s to %s", vuln.PkgName, vuln.FixedVersion)
133				}
134	
135				findings = append(findings, Finding{
136					ID:          vuln.VulnerabilityID,
137					Title:       vuln.Title,
138					Description: vuln.Description,
139					Severity:    parseSeverity(vuln.Severity),
140					Source:      "trivy",
141					File:        result.Target,
142					PkgName:     vuln.PkgName,
143					Version:     vuln.InstalledVersion,
144					FixedIn:     vuln.FixedVersion,
145					References:  refs,
146					FixCommand:  fixCmd,
147				})
148			}
149	
150			// Process licenses found by Trivy
151			for _, license := range result.Licenses {
152				findings = append(findings, Finding{
153					ID:          license.Name,
154					Title:       fmt.Sprintf("%s (%s)", license.PkgName, license.Name),
155					Description: fmt.Sprintf("License category: %s", license.Category),
156					Severity:    parseSeverity(license.Severity),
157					Source:      "trivy-license",
158					File:        license.FilePath,
159					PkgName:     license.PkgName,
160				})
161			}
162	
163			// Process misconfigurations found by Trivy
164			for _, misconf := range result.Misconfigurations {
165				var miscRefs []string
166				if misconf.PrimaryURL != "" {
167					miscRefs = append(miscRefs, misconf.PrimaryURL)
168				}
169				findings = append(findings, Finding{
170					ID:          misconf.AVDID,
171					Title:       misconf.Title,
172					Description: misconf.Desc,
173					Severity:    parseSeverity(misconf.Severity),
174					Source:      "trivy-misconfig",
175					File:        result.Target,
176					Line:        misconf.CauseMetadata.StartLine,
177					Resolution:  misconf.Resolution,
178					References:  miscRefs,
179				})
180			}
181		}
182	
183		return findings, nil
184	}

186	// parseSeverity converts string severity to SeverityLevel
187	func parseSeverity(s string) SeverityLevel {
188		switch strings.ToUpper(s) {
189		case "CRITICAL":
190			return SeverityCritical
191		case "HIGH":
192			return SeverityHigh
193		case "MEDIUM":

Extracting the subprocess seam collapsed two statements into one return:

```go
return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(tc.Name, cmd.Wait(), stderr.String())
```

Operands are evaluated before the call, so `stdout.Bytes()` snapshots the buffer
**before** `cmd.Wait()` runs — and `os/exec` fills that buffer from goroutines
only Wait is guaranteed to have finished. `Bytes()` returns a slice header with
the length at that moment, so later writes are invisible: the report was always
empty, every scan reported no findings, and the exit code alone survived. The
code it replaced got this right by accident of being written as separate
statements.

The read now lives in `finish`, after Wait, with the reasoning recorded next to
it so it is not re-collapsed. Pinned by `TestTheReportOnStdoutIsWhatComesBack`,
which is the test that failed first when the seam was finally exercised.

Worth stating plainly: this is the one defect in this list that the tests
*introduced* rather than merely found, and it never reached a commit. A
mechanical-looking refactor changed evaluation order, which is exactly what a
package with no tests under it cannot tell you.

Passe de couverture terminée. `internal/scan` : **45,5 % → 99,2 %**, global **71,9 % → 73,6 %**.

### Un vrai défaut trouvé — et c'était une régression du refactor non commité

Le split avait collapsé deux statements en un seul `return` :

```go
return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(tc.Name, cmd.Wait(), stderr.String())
```

Les opérandes sont évalués avant l'appel, donc `stdout.Bytes()` photographie le buffer **avant** `cmd.Wait()` — or `os/exec` le remplit depuis des goroutines que seul `Wait` garantit terminées. `Bytes()` renvoie un slice header avec la longueur du moment : **tous les scans revenaient vides**, seul le code de sortie survivait. Le code d'origine (`git show HEAD:internal/scan/trivy.go`) était correct par accident d'avoir été écrit en statements séparés.

La lecture vit maintenant dans `finish()`, après `Wait`, avec le raisonnement à côté pour qu'on ne la re-collapse pas. C'est le premier test écrit qui l'a fait tomber (`TestTheReportOnStdoutIsWhatComesBack`) — le seam existait depuis un commit entier sans que rien ne l'utilise, et c'est précisément dans cet écart que le défaut vivait.

### Ce qui a été écrit

| Fichier | Couvre |
|---|---|
| `run_test.go` | `cliRunner` **réel**, `waitErr`, `exitError`, `toolCmd.String` |
| `execute_test.go` | `RunTrivy`, `runTrivy`, `RunTrivyMisconfig`, `GenerateSBOM`, `RunGitleaks` |
| `scan_test.go` | `Scanner.Scan` — gating des étapes, agrégation, erreurs, progression |
| `dependencies_test.go` | `CheckDependenciesWithImages`, `checkDockerImage`, `NewScanner` |

Deux techniques réutilisables, consignées au backlog :

- **Le binaire de test tient le rôle de l'outil.** `TestMain` repère des variables d'environnement et se comporte en scanner (rapport sur stdout, progression sur stderr, code de sortie choisi). C'est ce qui couvre le runner *de production*, sans trivy ni gitleaks installés et sans compilateur au moment du test.
- **La détection est pilotée par le `PATH`.** Copier le binaire de test dans `t.TempDir()` sous les noms `trivy`/`gitleaks`/`docker` rend déterministes toutes les branches : binaire préféré à l'image, image absente, daemon injoignable, version illisible.

Cinq statements restent non couverts et le resteront : deux chemins d'erreur d'`AddToGitleaksIgnore` qui demanderaient un FS injecté, et un repli `StderrPipe` que `Run` ne peut pas atteindre.

### Vérifications

`go build` OK · `go test ./...` OK · `go vet` propre · `golangci-lint run ./...` → **0 issues** · `gofmt` propre.

Le détecteur de race reste indisponible localement (pas de gcc) — c'est la limitation déjà documentée, CI la couvre. Elle compte plus qu'avant : `Scanner.Scan` est le seul endroit de l'application qui fan-out sur des goroutines concurrentes écrivant un résultat partagé, et ses tests pilotent maintenant les cinq étapes en parallèle. **La confirmation est à lire sur la CI**, je ne peux pas l'obtenir ici.

Rien n'est commité — la phase 5 forme maintenant une PR complète (D19 + le refactor + la couverture + le backlog).
